strengths: Clear problem formulation: Well-demonstrates the 'complexity cliff' in VIT datasets where 90.1% of questions require ≤2 capabilities, providing strong motivation
Systematic data generation pipeline: Well-designed 4-step methodology with clear atomic capability taxonomy, quality verification, and natural integration constraints
Strong empirical results: Achieves 100.18% relative performance with only 10% of data; substantial improvements on complex tasks (e.g., +83.3% on MMStar for k≥4 tasks)
Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive ablation studies validating balanced k-distribution, capability coverage, complexity range, and instruction tuning ratio
Data efficiency demonstration: Convincingly shows COMPACT outperforms larger random baselines; 2K COMPACT model often exceeds 32K random baseline (Fig. 3)
Thorough analysis: Good per-complexity analysis (Fig. 4), leave-one-out analysis identifying critical capabilities, and clear demonstration of balanced k-distribution importance (Table 3)
Reproducibility: Detailed system prompts in appendix and commitment to release generated data
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core insight (compositional learning improves generalization) is well-established; contribution is primarily applying known principles to MLLM data curation rather than methodological innovation

Problematic circular dependency on closed-source models: Gemini-2.0-Flash used for generation, verification, and capability analysis; creates systemic bias and undermines reproducibility despite data release promise
No human evaluation: Capability labeling and question quality verified solely by Gemini; no inter-annotator agreement, human validation, or quality spot-checks of generated data
Limited compositional complexity range: Restricted to k≤3 due to Gemini's decreasing reliability; k>3 generalization is underexplored and claims of scalability are weakened
Weak performance on knowledge-intensive tasks: Marginal improvements on OK-VQA (+0.7%), MMMU (+1.0%), MMMU-Pro (+2.08%) contradict claims of 'scalable recipe' for general capabilities
No statistical significance testing: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; unclear if small improvements (e.g., +0.6% TextVQA) are statistically significant
Incomplete analysis: 'Natural integration' remains vague; why LLaVA-W has 3x higher average k than other benchmarks unexplained; no failure case analysis or prompt sensitivity study
Dataset assembly details: Only 49% of total training data (32K of 65K) is new compositional content; mixing with original VIT data makes contribution attribution less clear

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-illustrated 'complexity cliff' in standard VIT datasets
Systematic and thoughtful four-step data generation pipeline with reasonable quality constraints
Comprehensive evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with strong improvements on complex tasks (k≥4)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating that balanced k-distribution is the key driver of improvements
Compelling data efficiency story—matching full VIT performance with ~10% of data on several benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core insight (need for compositional data) is known; the execution is straightforward rather than conceptually novel

Critical reproducibility concerns: heavy reliance on closed-source Gemini 2.0-Flash makes work difficult to reproduce; generation costs not quantified; promised data release doesn't solve reproducibility for future work

Inconsistent and marginal overall results: improvements vary dramatically across benchmarks (0.8%-13.8%), with negative results on LLaVA-in-the-Wild (-3.7%); '100.18% relative score' claim is misleading—barely distinguishable from baseline, no statistical significance testing
Poor generalization beyond vision-centric tasks: minimal improvements on knowledge-intensive benchmarks (Table 4) reveals fundamental limitation; approach doesn't scale to modern MLLM requirements
Scalability limitations: data generation only supports k≤3 due to model reliability issues; unclear how well k≤3 training generalizes to higher-complexity reasoning; no clear path forward

Atomic capability taxonomy appears ad-hoc: lacks rigorous justification for the 10 chosen capabilities; no analysis of completeness or optimality; categorization into Attribution/Recognition/Relation is somewhat arbitrary
Comparison fairness concerns: COMPACT data is specifically curated to be compositional while baselines use generic selection, making it not a fully controlled comparison
No inter-annotator agreement or human evaluation of generated question quality; quality verification thresholds (70% confidence, 60% word overlap) are arbitrary and sensitivity is unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear demonstration of the 'complexity cliff' in existing VIT datasets (90.1% of LLaVA-665K questions require ≤2 capabilities)
Systematic and principled approach with well-grounded taxonomy of 10 atomic capabilities organized into clear categories
Comprehensive evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with substantial improvements on complex tasks (83.3% on MMStar k≥4, 94.0% on MM-Vet k≥4)
Excellent ablation studies validating all design choices: balanced complexity distribution (Table 3), complexity range (Fig 7), instruction tuning ratio (Fig 8), and capability coverage (Fig 6)
Strong data efficiency demonstrated: achieves 100.18% relative performance with only 10% of LLaVA-665K's data; 2K COMPACT samples often exceed 32K random VIT samples (Figure 3)
Fair experimental setup: uses same images as baseline, same model architecture and training configuration, appropriate baselines (Random, ICONS)
Clear technical execution with well-designed 4-step pipeline (capability sampling, generation, verification, assembly) and detailed quality control measures
Strong presentation with effective visualizations that clearly communicate the approach and results
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on closed-source Gemini-2.0-Flash for data generation and verification limits reproducibility, introduces potential biases, and creates vendor lock-in; limited exploration of sensitivity to prompt design or other LLMs

Training limited to k≤3 despite evaluation on k≥4 tasks; generalization to higher complexity levels is real but may be hitting fundamental limits; insufficient analysis of why k≥4 generation is unreliable

Weak performance on knowledge-intensive tasks (Table 4: OK-VQA, MMMU show only marginal improvements), making the 100.18% relative score an aggregate that masks inconsistent performance across task types
Quality verification methodology only via Gemini without human inter-rater reliability validation; confidence thresholds (70%) and word overlap filtering (60%) appear somewhat arbitrary
Limited conceptual novelty: core idea of compositional training is straightforward; contribution is primarily in systematic execution rather than fundamental innovation

Incomplete comparative analysis: only compares against Random and ICONS data selection; lacks comparison with other compositional approaches (CoT reasoning, multi-step prompting) or concurrent data selection methods

Benchmark-specific concerns: several benchmarks have low average k (InfoVQA k̄=0.34, SeedBench k̄=1.11), so COMPACT's advantages are not uniformly pronounced; 100.18% average is driven by specific benchmarks
Dataset assembly rationale underdeveloped: why 5% VIT mixture is optimal is shown empirically but not theoretically justified; claim about instruction-following orthogonality lacks support
Limited qualitative analysis: only 3 examples in Figure 11; no systematic error analysis or failure mode investigation
Missing analyses: scalability beyond 32K compositional samples, computational cost of generation vs. gains, transferability to other base models or encoders

strengths: Strong practical results: achieves 100.2% of full LLaVA-665K performance with only 10% data volume, with particularly impressive gains on complex benchmarks (MM-Vet +8.6%, MMStar +2.9%)

Well-structured atomic capabilities framework: 10 vision-centric capabilities organized into three clear categories (attribution, recognition, relation) with interpretable complexity measure (k-value)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 8 diverse benchmarks, 7 data selection baselines, extensive ablations isolating effects of k-value range, instruction tuning ratio, and complexity
Rigorous quality control and transparency: systematic 4-step pipeline with 21% rejection rate, detailed failure mode analysis, system prompts provided, promise to release data publicly
Thorough analysis with proper controls: COMPACTllava experiment isolates complexity effects, token-level analysis, capability distribution comparison, open-source baseline evaluation
weaknesses: Limited novelty: compositional/complex data augmentation is not new; the core insight that more complex questions improve learning is relatively intuitive, making this primarily an engineering contribution

Reproducibility severely hampered by closed-source dependency: entire pipeline requires Gemini-2.0-Flash ($86.5 per 32K samples); open-source alternative (Qwen3) shows notably worse performance (98.31% vs 100.18%), limiting practical adoption

Inconsistent improvements across benchmarks: performance actually decreases on TextVQA (96.0% relative), remains significantly below baseline on LLaVA-in-the-Wild (94.2%) and CV-Bench (90.7%), suggesting limited generalization

Substantial performance limitations on knowledge-intensive tasks: OK-VQA (86.3% relative), MMMU (100% but plateau), MMMU-Pro showing that method only works well for vision-centric tasks, significantly narrowing scope

Only ~50% of improvements attributable to complexity: COMPACTllava control experiment (Table 3) shows that of the 2.6% improvement over random baseline, only ~1.3% comes from higher k-values while ~1.3% comes from Gemini's superior question generation ability, questioning the core hypothesis

Atomic capabilities framework concerns: capabilities are not orthogonal (Fig. 8), object recognition implicitly assumed in most questions (Fig. 7), taxonomy may not be exhaustive or optimal, limited justification for these specific 10 capabilities
Limited architectural evaluation: only tested on LLaVA-7B-LoRA; unclear how findings generalize to different model sizes or architectures
Missing human evaluation: no assessment of synthetic question quality, naturalness, or actual difficulty; entire validation relies on automated metrics
Unvalidated core claim: no evidence that model learns genuine compositional reasoning versus simply learning better-engineered questions from Gemini

strengths: Clear motivation: Well-supported observation that VIT datasets over-represent simple questions (77% with k≤2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 8 benchmarks, 7 baseline comparisons, detailed ablations on k-value ranges and instruction tuning ratios
Practical improvements: Achieves 100.2% relative performance with 10x data reduction is noteworthy and would have real-world value
Thorough transparency: Extensive appendices with failure mode analysis, token efficiency analysis, capability ablations, and system prompts support understanding and reproducibility
Good scaling analysis (Fig. 3) demonstrating efficiency gains as compositional tuning data increases
weaknesses: Critical confounded comparison: COMPACT generates new questions with Gemini-2.0-Flash while baselines randomly select from existing LLaVA data. Table 9 shows Qwen3 generator reduces performance to 98.31% (vs 100.18% with Gemini), suggesting ~2% of gains come from generator choice, not complexity. The contribution of actual complexity is unclear.

Weak k-value complexity metric: (1) Determined subjectively by prompting Gemini, (2) Circular verification using Gemini to both generate and verify k-values, (3) Table 4 shows only modest correlation with difficulty (46.4% at k=1 vs 39.8% at k=3), (4) Capabilities are non-orthogonal (Fig. 8) undermining 'atomic' framing, (5) Object recognition implicitly assumed 50%+ of the time (Fig. 7)

No evidence of increased information utilization: Claims that higher-k questions encourage models to learn from more visual features lack support. No saliency maps, attention analysis, or feature usage comparison across k-values provided.

Narrow scope and generalization concerns: Only tested on LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA; no other model sizes/architectures evaluated. Single base dataset (LLaVA-665K). Knowledge-intensive tasks show only marginal gains. Performance on TextVQA actually regresses (44.37 vs 46.99). Heavy dependency on proprietary Gemini API.

Missing fair baseline: No comparison of Gemini-generated k=1,2 questions vs k=3 questions to isolate complexity effect from generation quality. No evaluation against other synthetic data generation methods.

Methodological issues: (1) 5% VIT mixture acts as implicit warm-start/regularizer—unclear contribution, (2) High rejection rates at high k (66.7% for kgen=3) suggest questions are forced/unnatural, (3) No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported, (4) Arbitrary hyperparameter choices (why kgen∈{1,2,3}?).

Incomplete results analysis: (1) 'Outperforms full dataset' claim holds only for MM-Vet and MMStar, not consistently across benchmarks, (2) Gains are often small (e.g., 2.9% on MMStar), (3) Performance plateaus after 16K samples (Fig. 3), (4) Missing ablation: which atomic capabilities actually drive improvements?

Questionable theoretical foundation: Conflates task complexity with information density. A complex question isn't necessarily more informative if it exercises similar visual features. The 'atomic' framing is misleading given non-orthogonality and implicit assumptions.

strengths: Clear problem motivation demonstrating that standard VIT datasets over-represent simple single-capability questions (k≈1.95) and under-utilize visual information
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse benchmarks with comparison against 8 data selection baselines, showing 100.2% relative performance at 10% data volume
Rigorous control experiments isolating complexity effects (Table 3 matching LLaVA distribution) and demonstrating efficient scaling (Figure 3)
Well-defined systematic 4-step data generation pipeline with transparent quality verification including confidence scoring, word overlap deduplication, and capability verification
Significant improvements on complex reasoning tasks (MM-Vet +8.6%, MMStar +2.9%, InfoVQA +13.8%) indicating effectiveness for compositional reasoning
Thorough ablation studies on k-value range and instruction tuning ratio, with detailed analysis of complexity distributions and failure modes
Practical value for reducing computational costs in MLLM training with promise to release generated data
Well-organized taxonomy of 10 atomic visual capabilities with clear categorization and extensive supplementary analysis
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on closed-source Gemini-2.0-Flash for data generation limiting reproducibility; open-source alternative (Qwen3) drops performance to 98.31%, and generation cost is substantial ($86.5 for 32K samples)
Limited evaluation scope: single model (LLaVA-v1.5-7B-LoRA) and checkpoint type (pre-VIT); no evaluation on larger models, other MLLMs, or specialized domains, raising questions about generalization

Atomic capability taxonomy lacks true orthogonality with object recognition implicitly assumed during generation (Figure 7, Appendix A.4), potentially biasing results toward object-centric questions; based solely on LLaVA-665K analysis
Significant performance degradation on knowledge-intensive tasks (Table 9: OK-VQA +0.72%, MMMU-Pro +2.08%) with only modest gains, limiting applicability to subset of VL tasks

Confounded interpretation from mixing 5% real VIT data with 95% synthetic data; ablation in Table 3 only uses 16K total data (vs. 65K main setup), unclear how much improvement is from synthetic vs. instruction formatting
Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; some improvements appear marginal (TextVQA 44.37 vs 46.99 baseline is worse)
k-value measurement relies on LLM analysis without human validation or inter-annotator agreement metrics; no evaluation of measurement reliability despite centrality to the method
Hyperparameter choices (70% confidence threshold, 60% word overlap, max 10 verification attempts, 2-3 conversations per kgen) lack justification or ablation studies
Missing comparisons with curriculum learning and other complexity-based training approaches; incomplete analysis of when and why COMPACT helps vs. when it doesn't
Training setup uses single epoch and LoRA fine-tuning which may limit learning capacity; uses pre-VIT checkpoint differing from published baseline, affecting reproducibility
